lines: Sweden studied lottery winners.
Men who won got married more often.
They had more children.
Women who won were more likely to divorce, at least for a while.
Researchers say the money didn't end those marriages.
It sped up the ones already ending.
reels.source: Cesarini, Lindqvist, Ostling, Terskaya, 'Fortunate Families?', Journal of Human Resources; reported by PsyPost
reels.caveat: short-run divorce effect only; Swedish data; strongest in recent weak-match marriages with husband as main earner

lines: You think you can spot a liar.
Researchers combined 206 studies.
People caught lies 54% of the time.
A coin flip is 50%.
We spot the truth 61% of the time.
We catch a lie 47% of the time.
reels.caveat: study counts differ between secondary sources

lines: After a spouse dies, the one left behind is more likely to die too.
In 373,189 older couples,
the risk was 30% to 90% higher in the first three months.
About 15% higher after that.
Scientists call it the widowhood effect.
reels.source: Elwert and Christakis, American Journal of Public Health 2008

lines: Divorce is falling in America.
Except after 50.
Between 1990 and 2010,
divorce among people 50 and older roughly doubled.
From about 5 to 10 per 1,000 married people.
reels.source: Brown and Lin, BGSU (Journals of Gerontology 2012); NPR coverage
reels.caveat: after 2010 the rate fell for ages 50-64 and kept rising for 65+
